oneLiner: Life-threatening bleed: 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg IV + vitamin K 5-10 mg IV slow. INR > 10 without bleeding: oral vitamin K 1-5 mg + hold. Never use FFP if PCC is available.
mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → depletes functional factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S. Reversal restores those factors directly (PCC) or via the liver over hours-to-days (vitamin K).

protocols.agent: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC, e.g. Beriplex, Kcentra, Octaplex)
protocols.dosing: INR 2-3.9: 25 IU/kg (max 2,500 IU). INR 4-5.9: 35 IU/kg (max 3,500 IU). INR ≥ 6: 50 IU/kg (max 5,000 IU). Round to nearest vial; give IV over 10-30 min. Repeat INR within 30 min and 6 h.
adjuncts: Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 5-10 mg IV slowly (dilute, infuse over ≥ 30 min — risk of anaphylactoid reaction with rapid bolus) — sustains reversal beyond PCC half-life.
Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid as per haemorrhage management.
Reverse hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia (lethal triad).
protocols.monitoring: INR at 30 min, 6 h, 24 h. Clinical bleeding endpoint. Watch for thrombosis post-PCC (especially in valve / DOAC-naïve patients).
cautions: Do NOT use FFP if 4F-PCC is available — slower, larger volume, less effective.
Activated PCC (FEIBA) is not first-line for warfarin reversal; reserve for specific factor inhibitor scenarios.
Mechanical heart valve: discuss with cardiology before reversal; thrombosis risk.

protocols.dosing: If surgery within 6-12 h: 4F-PCC dosed by INR as above PLUS vitamin K 5-10 mg IV. If surgery in 24-72 h: vitamin K 5-10 mg PO/IV may suffice; recheck INR before procedure.
adjuncts: Discuss thrombosis risk vs bleeding with the surgical team — bridging plan post-operatively.
protocols.monitoring: INR pre-procedure (target depends on procedure; < 1.5 for major surgery).

protocols.dosing: Hold warfarin. Vitamin K 5-10 mg IV slowly. Consider 4F-PCC 25 IU/kg if INR significantly elevated or bleeding persists despite local measures.
INR 4.5-10, no bleed: hold 1-2 doses, recheck INR; routine vitamin K not required. INR > 10, no bleed: vitamin K 1-5 mg PO; hold warfarin; recheck INR at 24 h. Restart at lower dose once therapeutic.
cautions: Avoid large doses (≥ 10 mg) of vitamin K in patients on long-term warfarin for thrombosis prophylaxis — risk of over-correction and warfarin resistance for days.

pitfalls: FFP requires ~ 30 mL/kg to fully reverse INR — usually impractical and volume-overloading; PCC is the standard of care where available.
Vitamin K alone takes 6-12 h to begin lowering INR — do not rely on it for active life-threatening bleeding.
Subcutaneous vitamin K is unreliable (erratic absorption) — use IV or oral.
After PCC, INR may rebound at 12-24 h once PCC factors decay — vitamin K supplementation prevents this.
Mechanical valve patients have a substantial early thrombosis risk after reversal — restart anticoagulation as soon as bleeding controlled, ideally with heparin bridge.

references.label: BSH guideline: Reversal of antithrombotic therapy in patients with major bleeding. Br J Haematol 2018.
Neurocritical Care Society / Society of Critical Care Medicine: Guideline for reversal of antithrombotics in intracranial haemorrhage. 2016.

oneLiner: Life-threatening bleed or urgent surgery: idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials). If idarucizumab unavailable: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg + dialysis (dabigatran is dialysable, ~ 60% removal in 4 h).
mechanism: Direct, reversible thrombin (IIa) inhibitor. Renally cleared (~ 80%) — accumulates in CKD. Half-life 12-17 h normal renal function; > 24 h if CrCl < 30 mL/min.

protocols.dosing: 5 g IV — given as two consecutive infusions or boluses of 2.5 g each, no more than 15 min apart. Onset within minutes; reversal sustained for up to 24 h.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid as per haemorrhage management.
Activated charcoal 50 g PO/NG if ingestion within 2 h AND airway protected.
Haemodialysis can be added in severe cases (especially CKD): removes ~ 60% in 4 h. Note: idarucizumab is NOT removed by dialysis.
protocols.monitoring: Dilute thrombin time (dTT), ecarin clotting time (ECT) if available, or aPTT (less sensitive); clinical bleeding endpoint. Re-bleeding within 24 h is described — anticipate possible repeat dosing.

protocols.dosing: Same as life-threatening bleed: 5 g IV (two 2.5 g aliquots). Proceed to surgery when reversal confirmed (normalised aPTT / dTT).
Hold dabigatran. Local haemostasis. Idarucizumab 5 g IV if bleeding persists or cannot be controlled. 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg if idarucizumab unavailable.
Hold 1-2 doses. Recheck renal function; review dose appropriateness. Reassess indication and bleeding risk.

pitfalls: Renal clearance dominates — CrCl < 30 mL/min: half-life > 24 h, expect prolonged effect even after idarucizumab.
Idarucizumab is a humanised monoclonal Fab fragment — short half-life (~ 47 min α, 10 h β); rebleeding due to dabigatran redistribution from tissues can occur 12-24 h post-reversal.
Normal aPTT does NOT rule out clinically significant dabigatran effect — use dTT or ECT.
PCC is less effective for dabigatran than for Xa-inhibitor reversal; idarucizumab is the standard of care where available.
Restart anticoagulation as soon as bleeding controlled to avoid thromboembolic complications (median 4-7 days post-bleed in published series).

references.label: Pollack CV Jr et al. Idarucizumab for dabigatran reversal — full cohort analysis. NEJM 2017;377:431-41.
Tomaselli GF et al. 2020 ACC expert consensus on management of bleeding in patients on oral anticoagulants. JACC 2020.

oneLiner: Life-threatening bleed: andexanet alfa (where available, dose by last apixaban dose + time since) OR 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg. Andexanet is procoagulant — anticipate VTE risk and rebound thrombosis.
mechanism: Direct, reversible factor Xa inhibitor. ~ 27% renal clearance; half-life 12 h. Reversal by sequestration (andexanet decoy receptor) or by bypassing (PCC supplies factor II/IX/X/VII).

protocols.dosing: Low dose (apixaban ≤ 5 mg AND last dose ≥ 8 h ago, OR unknown dose ≥ 8 h ago): 400 mg IV bolus over 15 min, then 4 mg/min infusion for up to 120 min. High dose (apixaban > 5 mg OR last dose < 8 h ago): 800 mg IV bolus over 30 min, then 8 mg/min infusion for up to 120 min.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid as per haemorrhage management.
Reverse hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia (lethal triad).
Restart anticoagulation as soon as bleeding controlled — andexanet's procoagulant effect raises rebound thrombosis risk significantly.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa activity (apixaban-calibrated if available — but anti-Xa is artefactually low during andexanet exposure due to assay interference). Clinical bleeding endpoint. VTE surveillance (incidence ~ 10% in ANNEXA-4 cohort).
cautions: Andexanet is contraindicated if the bleed is on apixaban for active VTE — risk of catastrophic clot.
Andexanet effect terminates within ~ 1-2 h of stopping infusion; apixaban can rebind once exogenous Xa is consumed.
Cost and availability are major barriers — 4F-PCC remains the standard where andexanet is unavailable.

protocols.dosing: 50 IU/kg IV (max 5,000 IU); some protocols use 25 IU/kg as initial dose with re-dosing. Round to nearest vial; give over 10-30 min.
adjuncts: Activated charcoal 50 g PO/NG if ingestion within 2-4 h AND airway protected.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV (10 min) then 1 g over 8 h for traumatic bleed (CRASH-2 logic).
Local haemostasis: endoscopy, IR embolisation, surgery.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa activity (apixaban-calibrated). Clinical bleeding endpoint. Thrombosis risk lower than with andexanet but not zero.

protocols.agent: Time-based: hold + delay if possible; andexanet or PCC if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Elective: hold 24-48 h (low bleed risk) or 48-72 h (high bleed risk, CrCl > 50). Urgent: andexanet (where available) or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg if bleeding intra-operatively.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (apixaban-calibrated) immediately preoperatively.

protocols.agent: Supportive + local haemostasis; consider 4F-PCC if persistent
protocols.dosing: Hold apixaban. Volume resuscitation. Activated charcoal within 2-4 h of ingestion. 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg if bleeding persists despite supportive care.
Hold 1-2 doses. Reassess indication, dose, and bleeding risk (HAS-BLED). Restart at appropriate dose.

pitfalls: INR and aPTT are unreliable measures of apixaban effect — use apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa.
Andexanet alfa interferes with anti-Xa assays — results during/immediately after infusion do NOT reflect true anticoagulant burden.
Andexanet has a black-box-equivalent warning for thromboembolic and ischaemic events — restart anticoagulation as soon as feasible.
Apixaban is NOT dialysable (high protein binding) — dialysis is not a reversal option.
Renal dose-reduction criteria (any 2 of: age ≥ 80, weight ≤ 60 kg, creatinine ≥ 133 µmol/L) — confirm dose was appropriate; supratherapeutic dosing in elderly is a common cause of bleeding.

references.label: Connolly SJ et al. Andexanet alfa for acute major bleeding associated with factor Xa inhibitors (ANNEXA-4). NEJM 2019;380:1326-35.
Tomaselli GF et al. 2020 ACC expert consensus on management of bleeding in patients on oral anticoagulants. JACC 2020.

oneLiner: Same approach as apixaban: andexanet alfa where available (low/high dose by last dose + time), or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg. Activated charcoal within 8 h of ingestion (longer absorption window than apixaban).
mechanism: Direct, reversible factor Xa inhibitor. ~ 33% renal clearance; half-life 5-13 h (longer in elderly / renal impairment). Highly protein-bound — not dialysable.

protocols.dosing: Low dose (rivaroxaban ≤ 10 mg AND last dose ≥ 8 h ago, OR unknown ≥ 8 h ago): 400 mg IV bolus over 15 min, then 4 mg/min for up to 120 min. High dose (rivaroxaban > 10 mg OR last dose < 8 h ago): 800 mg IV bolus over 30 min, then 8 mg/min for up to 120 min.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid.
Restart anticoagulation as soon as bleeding controlled — VTE rebound risk.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (rivaroxaban-calibrated; assay interference during andexanet). Clinical bleeding.

protocols.dosing: 50 IU/kg IV (max 5,000 IU), rounded to nearest vial. Activated charcoal 50 g PO/NG if ingestion within 8 h AND airway protected.
protocols.monitoring: Clinical bleeding; anti-Xa (rivaroxaban-calibrated).

protocols.agent: Hold and delay if possible; andexanet or 4F-PCC if cannot
protocols.dosing: Elective: hold 24-48 h (standard risk) or 48-72 h (high bleed risk / CrCl 30-50). Urgent: andexanet or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg if intra-operative bleeding.
Hold rivaroxaban. Activated charcoal within 8 h. 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg if persistent.
Hold 1-2 doses. Reassess dose appropriateness (especially CrCl 15-49: 15 mg OD; 50+: 20 mg OD with food).

pitfalls: Rivaroxaban has a longer absorption window than apixaban — activated charcoal useful up to 8 h post-ingestion.
Bioavailability depends on food (the 20 mg dose must be taken with food, otherwise ~ 66% absorption only).
PT may be prolonged but is an unreliable measure; use rivaroxaban-calibrated anti-Xa.
Not dialysable.
DOAC-on-DOAC bridging is common in errors — confirm the agent before reversal.

references.label: Connolly SJ et al. ANNEXA-4. NEJM 2019.
ISTH guidance: When and how to use idarucizumab and andexanet alfa. J Thromb Haemost 2020.

oneLiner: Andexanet not formally licensed for edoxaban in all jurisdictions; off-label use is reported. 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg is the practical reversal where andexanet unavailable.
mechanism: Direct, reversible factor Xa inhibitor. ~ 50% renal clearance; half-life 10-14 h. Reduced efficacy in patients with CrCl > 95 mL/min (paradoxically) — labelled for CrCl 15-95.

protocols.agent: 4F-PCC (first-line in most jurisdictions); andexanet off-label where considered
protocols.dosing: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg IV (max 5,000 IU). Andexanet off-label: high dose 800 mg + 8 mg/min infusion (extrapolated from rivaroxaban data).
adjuncts: Activated charcoal 50 g PO/NG within 2 h AND airway protected.
Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid.
Reverse lethal triad (hypothermia/acidosis/hypocalcaemia).
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (edoxaban-calibrated, if available); clinical bleeding.

protocols.agent: Hold ≥ 24 h (standard risk) / ≥ 48 h (high bleed risk); 4F-PCC if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Elective: hold 24-48 h. Urgent: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg if active bleeding.
Hold edoxaban. Activated charcoal within 2 h. 4F-PCC if persistent.
Hold 1-2 doses; reassess dose appropriateness.

pitfalls: Not licensed in some countries; check local availability and indication.
CrCl > 95: reduced efficacy in AF — consider alternative DOAC.
Not dialysable.
Andexanet labelling does not include edoxaban in many jurisdictions — use is off-label.

references.label: Tomaselli GF et al. 2020 ACC expert consensus on management of bleeding in patients on oral anticoagulants. JACC 2020.
ISTH guidance 2020.

oneLiner: Protamine sulfate 1 mg IV per 100 units of heparin given in the last 2-3 h, max 50 mg per dose, IV slowly. Anaphylaxis + hypotension common with rapid administration.
mechanism: Heparin potentiates antithrombin to inactivate thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa. Protamine binds heparin directly, forming an inactive complex.

protocols.dosing: 1 mg protamine IV per 100 units UFH given in the last 2-3 h. Maximum single dose 50 mg. Give slowly (over 10 min) — rapid administration causes hypotension, bradycardia, anaphylaxis. If UFH > 30 min ago, give 0.5 mg per 100 units (heparin half-life ~ 60-90 min IV).
adjuncts: Stop heparin infusion immediately.
Repeat aPTT 5-15 min after protamine; redose if still elevated (50% of initial dose).
Manage anaphylaxis: adrenaline, IV fluids, antihistamine, hydrocortisone.
protocols.monitoring: aPTT or anti-Xa. Clinical bleeding. Watch for hypotension during infusion.
cautions: Protamine is itself a weak anticoagulant in excess — do not over-dose.
Prior protamine exposure (CABG, NPH insulin users, vasectomy patients, fish allergy) increases anaphylaxis risk.

protocols.dosing: Stop UFH infusion 4-6 h before procedure for spontaneous decay (half-life ~ 90 min). Protamine if cannot delay or bleeding intra-operatively (post-cardiopulmonary-bypass dose ~ 1 mg / 100 units residual heparin).

pitfalls: Protamine dosing must account for time since last heparin dose (rapid IV elimination — 30 min ago: 0.5 mg/100 units; > 2 h: 0.25 mg/100 units).
After cardiopulmonary bypass, redistribution releases sequestered heparin (heparin rebound) 2-3 h later — re-dose protamine if aPTT rises again.
Anaphylaxis risk: prior CABG, NPH insulin (contains protamine), fish allergy.

references.label: Bates SM, Weitz JI. The mechanism of action of thrombin inhibitors. J Invasive Cardiol 2000.
Local trust protocol / BCSH guidelines.

anticoagulant: Low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin)
oneLiner: Protamine partially reverses LMWH (~ 60-75% anti-Xa neutralisation): 1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin (or per 100 anti-Xa units of other LMWH) given in the last 8 h; half-dose if 8-12 h ago.
mechanism: Antithrombin-potentiated anti-Xa activity > anti-IIa. Renal clearance — accumulates in CKD. Protamine fully reverses anti-IIa but only partially reverses anti-Xa (~ 60-75%) because of LMWH chain length variability.

protocols.dosing: Enoxaparin: 1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin if given within last 8 h; 0.5 mg per 1 mg if 8-12 h ago. Maximum single dose 50 mg. Give slowly (over 10 min). Dalteparin / tinzaparin: 1 mg protamine per 100 anti-Xa units. Repeat at half dose if bleeding persists.
adjuncts: Hold further LMWH.
Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid (1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h for traumatic / GI / mucosal bleeding).
Manage anaphylaxis risk as for protamine.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (LMWH-specific calibration). Clinical bleeding. Note: aPTT is INSENSITIVE to LMWH effect.

protocols.agent: Hold LMWH; protamine if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Prophylactic dose: hold 12 h pre-procedure. Therapeutic dose: hold 24 h pre-procedure (longer if CrCl < 30: 48 h). Protamine if active intra-operative bleeding.
Hold LMWH. Local haemostasis. Half-dose protamine (0.5 mg/mg or per 100 anti-Xa units) if bleeding persists.
Hold 1-2 doses. Reassess CrCl and weight-based dose.

pitfalls: Protamine never fully reverses LMWH — anti-Xa activity persists. Plan for ongoing bleeding management.
CrCl < 30: enoxaparin accumulates; use dose-adjusted regimen (1 mg/kg OD instead of BD) and consider switching to UFH for severe renal impairment.
Tinzaparin has the largest fraction reversible by protamine; nadroparin / dalteparin somewhat less.
aPTT is not a reliable monitor for LMWH — use anti-Xa (drawn 4 h post-dose, peak).

references.label: Tran HA et al. New oral anticoagulants — clinical management and reversal. Med J Aust 2014.
BCSH guideline: Reversal of antithrombotic therapy. Br J Haematol 2018.

drugClass: Synthetic pentasaccharide, indirect factor Xa inhibitor
oneLiner: No specific antidote — protamine ineffective. Activated PCC (aPCC / FEIBA) 20 IU/kg or recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) 90 µg/kg for life-threatening bleed; supportive care otherwise.
mechanism: Synthetic pentasaccharide that binds antithrombin selectively to inactivate factor Xa. Renally cleared; half-life 17-21 h (longer in elderly / renal impairment).

protocols.agent: Activated PCC (aPCC / FEIBA) or rFVIIa — limited evidence
protocols.dosing: aPCC 20 IU/kg IV (rounded to nearest vial). OR recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa, NovoSeven) 90 µg/kg IV bolus, repeat at 2 h if persistent bleeding.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid.
Stop fondaparinux.
Manage thromboembolic risk — both aPCC and rFVIIa are procoagulant; restart anticoagulation when bleeding controlled.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (fondaparinux-calibrated) if available — confirms drug level. Clinical bleeding endpoint.

protocols.agent: Hold ≥ 24 h (CrCl > 50) or 48-72 h (CrCl 30-50); aPCC / rFVIIa if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Elective: hold 24-72 h depending on CrCl. Urgent: aPCC 20 IU/kg or rFVIIa 90 µg/kg if intra-operative bleeding.
Hold fondaparinux. Local haemostasis. aPCC / rFVIIa only if persistent.
Hold 1-2 doses; reassess renal function and dose appropriateness.

pitfalls: Protamine does NOT reverse fondaparinux — do not use it.
Long half-life + renal accumulation in CKD — anticipate prolonged effect after stopping.
Limited evidence for aPCC / rFVIIa in fondaparinux reversal; both carry thrombosis risk.
Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30) — if reversal needed in a CKD patient, switch to UFH for future anticoagulation.

references.label: Bijsterveld NR et al. Recombinant factor VIIa reverses the anticoagulant effect of the long-acting pentasaccharide idraparinux. Br J Haematol 2004.
BCSH guideline 2018.

oneLiner: Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage post-tPA: stop infusion, cryoprecipitate 10 units IV + tranexamic acid 1-2 g IV. Neurosurgical consult immediately.
mechanism: Converts plasminogen to plasmin, lysing fibrin in clots. Causes systemic fibrinogenolysis; bleeding complications mediated by hypofibrinogenaemia and breakdown of haemostatic plugs.

protocols.dosing: Stop tPA infusion immediately. Cryoprecipitate 10 units (or 1 unit per 7-10 kg) IV — aim for fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L (some guidelines > 2.0). Tranexamic acid 1-2 g IV over 10 min. Recheck fibrinogen 30 min after cryoprecipitate; redose if < 1.5 g/L.
adjuncts: Send fibrinogen, prothrombin time, aPTT, platelets, group and screen STAT.
Platelets if count < 100 × 10⁹/L (particularly important in intracranial bleeds).
Neurosurgical consult for ICH within minutes.
Reverse hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia.
Blood pressure: target SBP 140-160 in tPA-related ICH (aggressive lowering risks ischaemic penumbra).
protocols.monitoring: Fibrinogen 30 min post-cryoprecipitate then 6 h. CT head repeat at 6-24 h. Neurological observations every 15 min for 2 h, then every 30 min for 6 h.
cautions: Aminocaproic acid (EACA) is an alternative if tranexamic acid unavailable — 4-5 g IV over 1 h.
Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is NOT effective for tPA-related bleeding (mechanism is fibrinogenolysis, not factor depletion).
Do not give FFP first-line — too slow and too low fibrinogen content; cryoprecipitate is much more efficient.

protocols.agent: Stop tPA; supportive + cryoprecipitate if persistent
protocols.dosing: Stop infusion. Local haemostasis. Cryoprecipitate 10 units if fibrinogen < 1.5 g/L AND bleeding persists.

pitfalls: tPA half-life is short (5 min) but fibrinogen depletion persists for hours — reversal is about replacing fibrinogen, not blocking the drug.
Time window for action is narrow — sICH after tPA carries 30-60% mortality.
Aggressive blood pressure lowering can extend ischaemic stroke — avoid SBP < 140 in tPA-related ICH.
Tenecteplase and reteplase reversal follows the same logic (cryoprecipitate + antifibrinolytic).
After successful reversal, anticoagulation restart depends on indication for thrombolysis — defer for ≥ 72 h post-haemorrhage unless competing thrombotic risk dominates.

references.label: Frontera JA et al. Guideline for reversal of antithrombotics in intracranial haemorrhage. Neurocrit Care 2016;24:6-46.
Powers WJ et al. AHA/ASA 2019 guideline for the early management of acute ischemic stroke.

drugClass: Antiplatelet — irreversible P2Y12 receptor antagonist (thienopyridine prodrug)
oneLiner: No specific antidote. Life-threatening bleed: stop drug + platelet transfusion (1 adult dose / 5 units RDP) — efficacy modest because circulating active metabolite continues to inhibit transfused platelets for ~ 6 h after last dose. Desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV is an adjunct.
mechanism: Prodrug activated by hepatic CYP2C19; active metabolite irreversibly binds the P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets. Effect lasts the lifespan of the affected platelets (7-10 days). Active metabolite has short plasma half-life (~ 30 min) but continues to be generated for hours after last dose.

protocols.dosing: Platelet transfusion: 1 adult therapeutic dose (typically pool of 4 units of pooled platelets or 1 apheresis unit) — consider 2 doses for intracranial haemorrhage. Desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 µg/kg IV over 30 min may improve platelet function (adjunct, not substitute). Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h for traumatic / mucosal bleeding.
adjuncts: Stop clopidogrel immediately.
Red cells, FFP as per haemorrhage management.
Local haemostasis: endoscopy, IR embolisation, surgery.
Reverse lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia).
protocols.monitoring: Clinical bleeding endpoint. Platelet function testing (VerifyNow P2Y12, PFA-100) is available in specialist centres but not widely standardised.
cautions: PATCH trial (Lancet 2016) showed platelet transfusion in spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage on antiplatelet therapy was associated with worse outcomes — discuss with neurosurgery / haematology before transfusing in spontaneous ICH.
Active metabolite continues to inhibit transfused platelets if given within ~ 6 h of last dose — defer transfusion if possible or anticipate need to redose.
Avoid antiplatelet restart for at least 72 h post-life-threatening bleed; longer for intracranial bleed.

protocols.agent: Hold ≥ 5-7 days if possible; platelet transfusion + desmopressin if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Elective surgery: hold 5-7 days. Urgent surgery: platelet transfusion at induction + intra-operatively if bleeding (1-2 adult doses). Desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV pre-op may reduce blood loss.

protocols.agent: Stop drug; supportive + tranexamic acid; platelets only if persistent
protocols.dosing: Stop clopidogrel. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV. Platelet transfusion only if bleeding persists despite supportive measures.
Hold 1-2 doses. Reassess indication, dual antiplatelet duration, and bleeding risk.

pitfalls: Irreversible inhibition — drug-free interval needed to restore platelet function; antidote does NOT exist.
Active metabolite continues to inhibit freshly transfused platelets if given within ~ 6 h of last clopidogrel dose.
PATCH trial cautions against platelet transfusion in spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage on antiplatelet therapy.
CYP2C19 poor metabolisers may have reduced clopidogrel effect (and so milder reversal need); ultra-rapid metabolisers have stronger effect.
Dual antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel + aspirin) post-stent: stopping both prematurely risks stent thrombosis — discuss with interventional cardiology.

references.label: Baharoglu MI et al. Platelet transfusion vs standard care for acute stroke due to spontaneous cerebral haemorrhage associated with antiplatelet therapy (PATCH). Lancet 2016;387:2605-13.
Levy JH et al. Reversal agents for non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants. Nat Rev Cardiol 2018.

oneLiner: Bentracimab (PB2452) is the specific reversal agent (where available) for life-threatening bleed. Otherwise stop drug, platelet transfusion limited by free circulating drug + active metabolite, tranexamic acid + supportive care.
mechanism: Reversible, non-competitive P2Y12 receptor antagonist. Parent drug + active metabolite (AR-C124910XX) both circulate. Half-life 7-9 h (parent) and 8-12 h (metabolite). Platelet transfusion less effective than for clopidogrel because circulating drug also inhibits transfused platelets.

protocols.agent: Bentracimab (specific reversal — where available) or platelet transfusion + supportive care
protocols.dosing: Bentracimab (PB2452, a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds ticagrelor): 18 g IV (typically a loading bolus + 4-hour infusion per product labelling) — restores platelet function within minutes. Availability is limited; check local supply. If unavailable: stop ticagrelor + platelet transfusion (efficacy modest; consider 2 adult doses for ICH) + tranexamic acid 1 g IV.
adjuncts: Stop ticagrelor immediately.
Red cells, FFP, fibrinogen replacement per major haemorrhage protocol.
Local haemostasis: endoscopy, IR, surgery.
Reverse lethal triad.
protocols.monitoring: Clinical bleeding endpoint. VerifyNow P2Y12 if available. After bentracimab: platelet function returns to baseline within minutes; sustained for 24 h.
cautions: Platelet transfusion is LESS effective than for clopidogrel because the circulating drug (parent + metabolite) inhibits transfused platelets — bentracimab is preferred where available.
Bentracimab is not dialysable; ticagrelor itself is highly protein-bound — dialysis ineffective.
PATCH trial caution applies to spontaneous ICH.

protocols.agent: Hold ≥ 3-5 days; bentracimab or platelet transfusion if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Elective surgery: hold 3-5 days (shorter than clopidogrel because reversible inhibition). Urgent: bentracimab if available, or platelet transfusion at induction.
Stop ticagrelor. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV. Platelet transfusion only if bleeding persists.
Hold 1-2 doses. Note ticagrelor BD dosing means missed-dose recovery is faster than clopidogrel.

pitfalls: Platelet transfusion is poorly effective for ticagrelor — the circulating drug + active metabolite inhibit fresh platelets.
Bentracimab is a specific antidote (REVERSE-IT programme) but not universally stocked — confirm availability locally before relying on it.
Dyspnoea is a common ticagrelor side-effect (not bleed-related) — do not mistake for tPA-style pulmonary haemorrhage.
Ticagrelor is a CYP3A4 substrate — interactions (strong inhibitors / inducers) change exposure significantly.
Cangrelor (IV, short-acting, reversible P2Y12) is sometimes used as a bridge in cardiac surgery — its effect washes out within 1 h of stopping infusion.

references.label: Bhatt DL et al. Antibody-based ticagrelor reversal agent in healthy volunteers (REVERSE-IT). NEJM 2019;380:1825-33.
Tomaselli GF et al. 2020 ACC expert consensus on management of bleeding in patients on oral anticoagulants. JACC 2020.

drugClass: Antiplatelet — irreversible P2Y12 receptor antagonist (thienopyridine prodrug, more potent than clopidogrel)
oneLiner: Like clopidogrel, irreversible — no specific antidote. Life-threatening bleed: stop drug + platelet transfusion (often 2 adult doses required because of greater inhibition). Active metabolite has very short plasma half-life (< 30 min) so transfused platelets less impaired by residual drug than with clopidogrel.
mechanism: Prodrug rapidly converted by intestinal and hepatic esterases / CYP3A4-CYP2B6 to an active thiolactone that irreversibly binds P2Y12. More potent and consistent inhibition than clopidogrel; less variability between patients.

protocols.dosing: Platelet transfusion 1-2 adult therapeutic doses (more inhibition than clopidogrel — anticipate higher requirement). Desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV as adjunct. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h.
adjuncts: Stop prasugrel.
Red cells, FFP, fibrinogen per major haemorrhage protocol.
Local haemostasis: endoscopy, IR, surgery.
protocols.monitoring: Clinical bleeding. VerifyNow P2Y12 if available.
cautions: Prasugrel is contraindicated in patients with prior stroke / TIA — bleeding-on-prasugrel in such a patient is a major prescribing red flag.
PATCH trial caution applies to spontaneous ICH on antiplatelet therapy.
Active metabolite half-life is short (< 30 min) — platelet transfusion 4-6 h after last dose is more effective than for clopidogrel.

protocols.agent: Hold ≥ 7 days if possible; platelet transfusion if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Elective: hold 7 days (longer than clopidogrel because more potent inhibition). Urgent: platelet transfusion at induction.
Stop prasugrel. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV.
Hold 1-2 doses; reassess weight-based dosing (5 mg/day if < 60 kg or ≥ 75 years).

pitfalls: Prasugrel is the most potent oral P2Y12 inhibitor in routine use — bleeding events are more severe than with clopidogrel.
Contraindicated in prior stroke / TIA — if patient has had bleed on prasugrel, check indication.
Reduced dose 5 mg/day for weight < 60 kg or age ≥ 75; supratherapeutic dosing in elderly underweight is a common contributor.
Irreversible inhibition — no antidote. Drug-free interval required.

references.label: Wiviott SD et al. Prasugrel versus clopidogrel in patients with acute coronary syndromes (TRITON-TIMI 38). NEJM 2007;357:2001-15.
BSH guideline 2018.

drugClass: Antiplatelet — irreversible COX-1 inhibitor (also salicylate at high dose)
oneLiner: Low-dose antiplatelet bleed: stop drug + platelet transfusion for life-threatening / intracranial bleed (PATCH caution for spontaneous ICH). Desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV is a useful adjunct. High-dose (analgesic / overdose) — also consider salicylate toxicity management.
mechanism: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 → ↓ thromboxane A2 → impaired platelet aggregation for the platelet lifespan (7-10 days). Effect at antiplatelet dose is selective for platelet COX-1.

protocols.dosing: Platelet transfusion 1 adult therapeutic dose (1-2 doses for ICH). Desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV over 30 min (also useful in uraemic platelet dysfunction). Tranexamic acid 1 g IV.
adjuncts: Stop aspirin.
Red cells, FFP per major haemorrhage protocol.
Local haemostasis.
protocols.monitoring: Clinical bleeding. VerifyNow Aspirin / PFA-100 in specialist centres.
cautions: PATCH trial — platelet transfusion in spontaneous ICH on antiplatelet therapy associated with worse outcomes; discuss with neurosurgery / haematology.
Plasma aspirin half-life is short (~ 20 min) — transfused platelets are not significantly impaired after a few hours.
High-dose ingestion (overdose): treat salicylate toxicity in parallel (bicarbonate, dialysis indications).

protocols.agent: Stop ≥ 5-7 days for elective; continue + platelet transfusion if vascular indication and cannot stop
protocols.dosing: Elective non-cardiac surgery: stop 5-7 days unless ischaemic risk dominates. Cardiac / vascular surgery: often continued — platelet transfusion intra-operatively if bleeding.
Stop aspirin. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV. Platelet transfusion only if bleeding persists.
Hold 1-2 doses. Reassess indication (primary prevention indications now narrowed).

pitfalls: Continuing aspirin peri-operatively is appropriate in many vascular / cardiac contexts despite the small bleeding increment — do not reflexively stop.
Combination antiplatelet / anticoagulant (e.g. DAPT + DOAC) compounds bleeding — discuss stepwise plan.
High-dose aspirin overdose — salicylate toxicity management (alkalinisation, dialysis) takes priority over antiplatelet reversal.
PATCH trial caution for spontaneous ICH.
Recent primary-prevention deprescribing trends — confirm indication before reversal.

references.label: Baharoglu MI et al. PATCH. Lancet 2016.
BSH guideline 2018.

drugClass: Antiplatelet — phosphodiesterase / adenosine reuptake inhibitor (often combined with aspirin)
oneLiner: Modest antiplatelet effect; usually co-formulated with aspirin (Aggrenox / Asasantin). Stop drug; manage bleeding largely as for aspirin (platelet transfusion only for severe bleed, desmopressin adjunct).
mechanism: Inhibits platelet phosphodiesterase (↑ cAMP) and adenosine reuptake (↑ extracellular adenosine acting on A2A receptors) → vasodilation + mild antiplatelet effect. Half-life ~ 10 h (extended-release).

protocols.agent: Stop drug; treat predominantly as aspirin bleed
protocols.dosing: Stop dipyridamole (and aspirin if combination product). Platelet transfusion 1-2 adult doses for ICH. Desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV.
adjuncts: Red cells, FFP per major haemorrhage protocol.
Local haemostasis.
Headache and hypotension are common dipyridamole side-effects — distinguish from neurological deterioration.
protocols.monitoring: Clinical bleeding.

protocols.dosing: Elective: hold 24-48 h (much shorter than thienopyridines because the antiplatelet effect is reversible and milder). Urgent: platelet transfusion if active bleeding.
Stop dipyridamole. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid.
Hold 1-2 doses; reassess indication (mainly secondary stroke prevention).

pitfalls: Bleeding risk is largely driven by the aspirin component of combination products, not the dipyridamole.
Vasodilatory headache is very common — do not over-investigate as ICH unless other neurological features.
Patients with severe coronary disease or aortic stenosis: dipyridamole-induced vasodilation can precipitate ischaemia.
Use with adenosine in cardiac stress testing — potentiates effect; do not co-administer therapeutic adenosine.

references.label: Diener HC et al. European Stroke Prevention Study 2 (ESPS-2). J Neurol Sci 1996.
BSH guideline 2018.

oneLiner: Used for intermittent claudication. Modest antiplatelet effect; stop drug for any bleed, platelet transfusion only for life-threatening haemorrhage. Half-life 11-13 h.
mechanism: Selective phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor → ↑ platelet cAMP (antiplatelet) and vascular smooth-muscle relaxation (vasodilation). CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 substrate.

protocols.agent: Stop drug + platelet transfusion if needed
protocols.dosing: Stop cilostazol. Platelet transfusion 1 adult dose if severe bleed. Desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV adjunct. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV.
adjuncts: Red cells, FFP per haemorrhage protocol.
Local haemostasis.
protocols.monitoring: Clinical bleeding.
cautions: Contraindicated in heart failure (any class) — PDE-3 inhibitors worsen mortality in HF.
If a HF patient is bleeding on cilostazol, check prescribing appropriateness.

protocols.dosing: Hold 48-72 h pre-procedure. Continue if peripheral revascularisation is urgent.
Stop cilostazol. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid.
Hold 1-2 doses. Headache (very common) is often dose-limiting; consider stepping down.

pitfalls: Contraindicated in heart failure — black-box warning in many jurisdictions.
Strong CYP3A4 / CYP2C19 inhibitors (ketoconazole, omeprazole) raise levels — review interactions.
Effect on hard cardiovascular endpoints is modest; main use is claudication symptom relief.

references.label: Bedenis R et al. Cilostazol for intermittent claudication. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014.
BSH guideline 2018.

oneLiner: No specific antidote. Half-life 40-50 min (longer in hepatic impairment). Life-threatening bleed: stop infusion + supportive; consider 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg or rFVIIa as last resort. Used primarily in HIT.
mechanism: Synthetic, reversible, direct inhibitor of thrombin (free and clot-bound). Hepatic clearance via CYP3A — accumulates in hepatic impairment. Short half-life 40-50 min; effect dissipates rapidly after stopping.

protocols.agent: Stop infusion + supportive; 4F-PCC / rFVIIa as last resort
protocols.dosing: STOP infusion immediately — effect wanes within 1-2 h (longer if hepatic impairment). 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg IV if bleeding refractory (limited evidence). Recombinant factor VIIa 90 µg/kg IV as rescue.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid per haemorrhage management.
Hepatic dysfunction: anticipate prolonged effect (half-life up to 3-4 h).
protocols.monitoring: aPTT (used for routine monitoring), ECT or dilute thrombin time if available. INR is artefactually elevated on argatroban — do not be misled.
cautions: Argatroban interferes with INR — transitioning back to warfarin requires overlapping for at least 4-5 days and stopping argatroban to interpret a true INR.
Limited evidence for PCC / rFVIIa rescue — discuss with haematology.
Not dialysable to a clinically useful extent.

protocols.agent: Stop infusion 2-4 h pre-procedure (longer if hepatic)
protocols.dosing: Stop infusion. Effect dissipates within 2-4 h with normal hepatic function; up to 12 h in hepatic impairment. Recheck aPTT pre-procedure.
Stop infusion. Effect wanes within 1-2 h. Local haemostasis.
Halve infusion rate or pause; recheck aPTT in 1-2 h.

pitfalls: Hepatic impairment markedly prolongs effect — start at 0.5 µg/kg/min (vs standard 2 µg/kg/min) in moderate-severe hepatic dysfunction.
INR is artefactually elevated — bridging back to warfarin is technically demanding.
Argatroban is one of the standard anticoagulants for HIT — bleeding patient with thrombocytopenia: consider underlying HIT diagnosis.
Not dialysable; no specific antidote.

references.label: Linkins LA et al. Treatment and prevention of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (CHEST). 2012;141(2 Suppl):e495S-e530S.
Cuker A et al. American Society of Hematology 2018 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: HIT. Blood Adv 2018.

oneLiner: No specific antidote. Very short half-life (~ 25 min, normal renal function). Stop infusion + supportive care; effect wanes within 1-2 h. 4F-PCC as last resort. Commonly used in PCI and HIT.
mechanism: Synthetic bivalent direct thrombin inhibitor — binds both the catalytic and substrate-recognition sites of thrombin. Primarily proteolytic / renal clearance. Half-life ~ 25 min (1 h if CrCl 30-60; 3-4 h if dialysis-dependent).

protocols.agent: Stop infusion + supportive; 4F-PCC as last resort
protocols.dosing: STOP infusion — effect wanes within 1-2 h in normal renal function. 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg IV if bleeding refractory.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid.
Haemodialysis removes ~ 25% in 4 h — adjunct in severe renal impairment.
Reverse lethal triad.
protocols.monitoring: aPTT or activated clotting time (ACT — used during PCI). Clinical bleeding.
cautions: Renal impairment significantly prolongs effect — dose-reduce accordingly.
Limited evidence for PCC; haemodialysis modestly effective.

protocols.agent: Stop infusion 1-2 h pre-procedure (longer if renal impairment)
protocols.dosing: Stop infusion. Effect dissipates within 1-2 h normal renal function; up to 6-8 h if dialysis-dependent.
Stop infusion. Local haemostasis.
Halve infusion rate or pause.

pitfalls: Short half-life means stopping is the most effective 'reversal' — anticipate effect to wane within 1-2 h.
Renal impairment dose-reduction is essential — accumulation causes prolonged bleeding.
ACT is monitored during PCI but not standardised for medical use.
Used in HIT — bleeding patient with thrombocytopenia: consider underlying HIT.

references.label: Linkins LA et al. Treatment and prevention of HIT (CHEST). 2012.
Stone GW et al. Bivalirudin during primary PCI in acute myocardial infarction (HORIZONS-AMI). NEJM 2008.

oneLiner: No specific antidote; protamine ineffective. Stop infusion + supportive; consider plasmapheresis for severe bleed (long half-life ~ 25 h). Used in HIT where available.
mechanism: Mixture of glycosaminoglycans (heparan, dermatan, chondroitin sulfate) potentiating antithrombin against factor Xa (predominantly) and IIa. Renal clearance; long anti-Xa half-life ~ 25 h. Minimal cross-reactivity with HIT antibodies (~ 10%).

protocols.agent: Stop infusion + supportive; plasmapheresis if refractory
protocols.dosing: Stop danaparoid. Supportive care. Plasmapheresis can remove the drug in severe refractory bleeding. Recombinant factor VIIa 90 µg/kg IV as rescue (limited evidence).
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid per haemorrhage management.
Long half-life means effect persists for ≥ 24 h after stopping.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (danaparoid-calibrated if available; ordinary LMWH-calibrated anti-Xa is suboptimal). Clinical bleeding.
cautions: PROTAMINE DOES NOT REVERSE DANAPAROID — do not use.
Cross-reactivity with HIT antibodies in ~ 10% — check before starting; if HIT serology is positive, choose argatroban / bivalirudin / fondaparinux.

protocols.dosing: Stop ≥ 48 h pre-procedure; recheck anti-Xa.
Stop danaparoid. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid.
Hold; reassess renal function and dose.

pitfalls: Protamine ineffective.
Long half-life (~ 25 h) — anticipate prolonged bleeding.
Limited global availability; withdrawn in several markets.
Cross-reactivity with HIT antibodies in a minority — confirm serology if HIT suspected.

references.label: Magnani HN, Gallus A. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT): a report of 1,478 clinical outcomes of patients treated with danaparoid (Orgaran) from 1982 to mid-2004. Thromb Haemost 2006.
BSH guideline 2018.

oneLiner: Long half-life (19-27 h), predominantly biliary clearance. 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg for life-threatening bleed; andexanet is not specifically labelled for betrixaban. Withdrawn from several markets — confirm local availability.
mechanism: Direct, reversible factor Xa inhibitor. Biliary clearance predominant (~ 80%); only ~ 11% renal — less renal-impairment dependent than other DOAC-Xa. Long half-life 19-27 h.

protocols.dosing: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg IV (max 5,000 IU). Activated charcoal 50 g PO/NG within 2 h AND airway protected.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid.
Reverse lethal triad.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (calibration may be difficult; rivaroxaban-calibrated as surrogate). Clinical bleeding.
cautions: Betrixaban withdrawn from several markets in 2020-2022 — confirm local availability.
Long half-life means prolonged effect after stopping; ongoing risk of rebleeding.

protocols.dosing: Elective: hold 72 h (long half-life). Urgent: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg.
Hold betrixaban. 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg if bleeding persists.
Hold 1-2 doses.

pitfalls: Limited clinical experience; withdrawn from several markets.
Long half-life — anticipate prolonged effect.
Not dialysable.
Andexanet labelling does NOT include betrixaban.

references.label: Cohen AT et al. Extended thromboprophylaxis with betrixaban in acutely ill medical patients (APEX). NEJM 2016.
ISTH guidance 2020.

anticoagulant: Warfarin — elective procedure, low bleed risk
oneLiner: Low-bleed-risk procedures (cataract, dental extraction, joint injection, simple skin biopsy): CONTINUE warfarin where INR therapeutic; no reversal needed. Stopping risks thromboembolism.
mechanism: Many minor procedures cause minimal bleeding controllable by local measures; the thromboembolic risk of stopping warfarin (especially in mechanical valves, recent VTE, CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 4) outweighs the small bleeding increment.

protocols.agent: Treat as warfarin major bleed (4F-PCC + vitamin K)
protocols.dosing: If unexpected major haemorrhage occurs intra-procedurally: 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg IV by INR + vitamin K 5-10 mg IV slow. See warfarin-reversal record.

protocols.agent: Continue warfarin; confirm INR in therapeutic range pre-procedure
protocols.dosing: Check INR within 24-72 h pre-procedure; if therapeutic (target range for indication), CONTINUE warfarin. Most dental procedures, cataract surgery, joint/soft-tissue injections, endoscopy WITHOUT biopsy, pacemaker / ICD generator change can be done safely on therapeutic warfarin.
adjuncts: Local haemostasis: tranexamic acid mouthwash (4.8% 10 mL, swill 2 min, do not swallow) post-dental extraction.
Pressure dressings, local cautery as required.
Inform proceduralist patient is anticoagulated.
cautions: Confirm INR in therapeutic range — supratherapeutic INR (> 4) warrants discussion / brief hold.
Mechanical valves and recent VTE / stroke: NEVER stop warfarin without discussing bridging.

protocols.dosing: Local pressure, tranexamic acid mouthwash for dental, suture removal as planned.

pitfalls: Reflexive stopping for low-bleed-risk procedures causes more thromboembolic harm than bleeding benefit.
Supratherapeutic INR (> 4) at procedure time: hold 1-2 doses; vitamin K only if very high.
Some 'low-bleed' procedures (e.g. transrectal prostate biopsy, complex skin excision over large area) are actually moderate / high bleed risk — confirm with proceduralist.
Mechanical valve patients with INR therapeutic on warfarin: do NOT bridge with LMWH for minor procedures — increases bleeding without thrombosis benefit (BRIDGE trial).

references.label: Douketis JD et al. Perioperative bridging anticoagulation in patients with atrial fibrillation (BRIDGE). NEJM 2015;373:823-33.
ACC/AHA 2017 perioperative management of anticoagulation guideline.

anticoagulant: Warfarin — elective major surgery, high bleed risk
oneLiner: Hold warfarin 5 days pre-procedure; bridge with LMWH ONLY if high thromboembolic risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent VTE < 3 months, CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 7 with prior stroke). BRIDGE trial: routine bridging for AF causes more bleeding without VTE benefit.
mechanism: High-bleed-risk procedures (major intra-abdominal, intracranial, spinal, urological, cardiothoracic) need INR < 1.5 to minimise haemorrhage. Stopping warfarin for 5 days normalises INR in most patients; thromboembolic risk during the gap is mitigated by bridging only when truly high.

protocols.dosing: If INR elevated intra-op and bleeding: 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg + vitamin K 5-10 mg IV slow. See warfarin-reversal.

protocols.agent: Hold warfarin 5 days; bridge LMWH only if high thromboembolic risk
protocols.dosing: Hold warfarin 5 days pre-procedure. Check INR 24 h pre-op — if > 1.5, give vitamin K 1-2 mg PO. LMWH bridging (therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD or dalteparin 100 IU/kg BD) ONLY for HIGH thromboembolic risk: mechanical mitral valve, any mechanical valve + AF / prior stroke, VTE within 3 months, CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 7 with prior stroke. Last LMWH dose: 24 h pre-op (half-dose only if therapeutic dose).
adjuncts: Restart warfarin 12-24 h post-op once haemostasis confirmed; resume LMWH 24-48 h post-op (later if neuraxial anaesthesia / high-bleed surgery), continue until INR therapeutic for 2 days.
Confirm INR < 1.5 pre-procedure; if not, vitamin K + delay if possible.
cautions: BRIDGE trial (NEJM 2015): for most AF patients, no bridging is non-inferior for thromboembolism and significantly reduces bleeding — DO NOT bridge routinely.
Neuraxial anaesthesia: hold therapeutic LMWH ≥ 24 h, prophylactic LMWH ≥ 12 h pre-block.
Restart timing depends on bleeding control + neuraxial considerations.

protocols.agent: Hold warfarin; supportive + selective vitamin K
protocols.dosing: Hold warfarin. Local haemostasis. Vitamin K 1-2 mg PO if INR > 4.
Hold 1-2 doses; reassess INR.

pitfalls: Routine bridging for AF causes more bleeding without thromboembolic benefit (BRIDGE trial).
Mechanical mitral valve is a strong indication for bridging — discuss with cardiology if uncertain.
Restarting warfarin too soon post-op risks haematoma; waiting too long risks thrombosis — typical restart 12-24 h once haemostasis confirmed.
Vitamin K > 5 mg pre-procedure causes prolonged warfarin resistance — use minimum effective dose (1-2 mg).

references.label: Douketis JD et al. BRIDGE. NEJM 2015;373:823-33.
ACC/AHA 2017 perioperative anticoagulation guideline.

oneLiner: DOACs DO NOT need LMWH bridging. Hold by half-life: standard risk apixaban / rivaroxaban / edoxaban 24-48 h, dabigatran 24-72 h (longer if renal). High-bleed-risk procedure: double those windows. PAUSE trial supports this approach.
mechanism: DOACs have short, predictable half-lives — stopping for 2-5 half-lives reduces drug effect to a level safe for surgery. Bridging is NOT required (and causes excess bleeding); it actively harmed patients in early DOAC peri-op protocols.

protocols.agent: Intra-operative haemorrhage: specific reversal (idarucizumab / andexanet) or 4F-PCC
protocols.dosing: Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV. Apixaban / rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa (low or high dose depending on last dose + time) or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg. Edoxaban / betrixaban: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg. See specific anticoagulant reversal records.

Standard bleed risk: Apixaban / rivaroxaban / edoxaban — hold ≥ 24 h (CrCl > 50). Dabigatran — hold ≥ 24 h (CrCl > 80), 36 h (CrCl 50-80), 48 h (CrCl 30-50), 72 h (CrCl < 30). HIGH bleed risk (intracranial, spinal, cardiothoracic, major abdominal): Apixaban / rivaroxaban / edoxaban — hold ≥ 48 h (CrCl > 50). Dabigatran — hold ≥ 48 h (CrCl > 80), 72 h (50-80), 96 h (30-50). Last dose of DOAC: 36-48 h before procedure depending on agent. NO LMWH bridging is given.
adjuncts: Restart DOAC: prophylactic-equivalent dose 24 h post-op (low bleed risk); therapeutic dose 48-72 h post-op (high bleed risk) — confirm haemostasis.
Neuraxial anaesthesia: hold ≥ 48-72 h for DOAC; longer if renal impairment.
PAUSE trial (Douketis 2019) validated this approach for AF patients undergoing surgery / procedures.
cautions: DO NOT BRIDGE WITH LMWH — increases bleeding without reducing thromboembolism.
Renal impairment requires longer hold periods (especially dabigatran).
Confirm last dose timing — patients self-report unreliably; check pharmacy refill data if uncertain.

protocols.dosing: Hold DOAC. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid. Consider 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg if bleeding persists (life-threatening track).
Hold 1-2 doses; reassess renal function and dose appropriateness.

pitfalls: Bridging DOACs with LMWH is INCORRECT and increases bleeding — never do this.
Dabigatran is most affected by renal impairment — extend hold periods accordingly.
DOAC restart too early increases bleeding — wait until surgical haemostasis confirmed.
Neuraxial anaesthesia mandates longer holds — discuss with anaesthesia.
PAUSE trial set the modern peri-op standard — review local protocol alignment.

references.label: Douketis JD et al. Perioperative management of patients with atrial fibrillation receiving a direct oral anticoagulant (PAUSE). JAMA Intern Med 2019;179:1469-78.
EHRA 2021 practical guide on the use of NOACs in patients with atrial fibrillation.

anticoagulant: Mechanical heart valve patient on warfarin — bleed
oneLiner: Reverse the bleed but plan re-anticoagulation early — mechanical valves have substantial early valve thrombosis risk. 4F-PCC + minimal vitamin K (1-2 mg, avoid > 5 mg to preserve future warfarin sensitivity); IV heparin bridge restart within 24-48 h.
mechanism: Mechanical valves (especially older-generation mitral valves) have a thromboembolic stroke risk of ~ 4-12% per year without anticoagulation. After reversal, valve thrombosis can occur within days; planned, time-limited reversal + early bridging is the standard.

protocols.agent: 4F-PCC + minimal vitamin K + cardiology / cardiac surgery consult
protocols.dosing: 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg IV by INR (as warfarin-reversal). Vitamin K 1-2 mg IV slowly (avoid 5-10 mg to preserve future warfarin sensitivity). Urgent cardiology / cardiac surgery consult.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid per haemorrhage management.
Plan IV heparin bridge to restart 24-48 h post-bleed once haemostasis confirmed.
Echocardiogram to assess valve thrombus if suspicious symptoms.
protocols.monitoring: INR, valve auscultation, echocardiography. Clinical bleeding endpoint.
cautions: Avoid large doses of vitamin K (≥ 5 mg) — produces prolonged warfarin resistance, delaying re-anticoagulation by days.
Mechanical mitral valves > mechanical aortic valves for thrombosis risk.
Older-generation mechanical valves (caged-ball, single-tilting-disc) have higher thrombosis risk than modern bileaflet.
Bridging with LMWH is acceptable in some cases but IV heparin preferred for ease of reversal if rebleeding.

protocols.dosing: Hold warfarin, vitamin K 1-2 mg, start IV UFH (aPTT 1.5-2x baseline) once procedure-related bleeding risk acceptable. Stop UFH 4-6 h pre-procedure; restart 6-12 h post-op once haemostasis confirmed.
Hold warfarin. Vitamin K 1-2 mg PO. 4F-PCC 25 IU/kg if persistent. Restart anticoagulation ASAP.

protocols.agent: Hold dose; minimal vitamin K only if INR very high
protocols.dosing: Hold 1-2 doses. Vitamin K 1 mg PO if INR > 10 (avoid larger doses). Target INR per valve type (typically 2.5-3.5 for mitral mechanical, 2.0-3.0 for aortic bileaflet).

pitfalls: DOACs are CONTRAINDICATED in mechanical heart valves (RE-ALIGN trial halted early due to thrombosis on dabigatran).
Vitamin K > 5 mg causes prolonged warfarin resistance — keep doses small in this group.
Routine reversal without re-anticoagulation plan risks valve thrombosis and embolic stroke.
Target INR depends on valve type and position — confirm before reversal.
Bridging with LMWH is acceptable for elective procedures but IV UFH is preferred for emergency / unpredictable rebleeding.

references.label: Eikelboom JW et al. Dabigatran versus warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves (RE-ALIGN). NEJM 2013;369:1206-14.
Nishimura RA et al. 2017 AHA/ACC focused update of the 2014 guideline for management of patients with valvular heart disease.

drugClass: Anticoagulation in pregnancy — special scenario (LMWH preferred; warfarin / DOACs avoided)
oneLiner: Pregnancy: LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice (does not cross placenta); warfarin teratogenic in T1, DOACs avoided. Life-threatening bleed: protamine partial reversal of LMWH + obstetric haemorrhage protocol. Senior obstetric / haematology / anaesthesia input early.
mechanism: LMWH does not cross the placenta — safe for fetus. Warfarin crosses (teratogenic embryopathy weeks 6-12, fetal haemorrhage T3). DOACs cross placenta and are insufficiently studied — avoid. Reversal in pregnancy must account for two patients, altered pharmacokinetics, and risk of placental abruption.

protocols.dosing: Stop LMWH immediately. Protamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin given in last 8 h; half-dose if 8-12 h ago (partial reversal — see LMWH-reversal). Activate major obstetric haemorrhage protocol: red cells (O-neg if urgent), FFP, platelets, fibrinogen / cryoprecipitate, tranexamic acid 1 g IV (WOMAN trial — within 3 h of postpartum haemorrhage onset).
adjuncts: Senior obstetric / anaesthesia / haematology input.
If on warfarin (rare in pregnancy, mainly mechanical valves): 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg + vitamin K 5-10 mg IV slow.
Cell salvage may be appropriate; do not delay reversal pending consent.
Consider perimortem caesarean if maternal cardiac arrest and gestation > 20 weeks.
protocols.monitoring: Fibrinogen (normal in pregnancy is higher — aim > 2 g/L), platelets, lactate, base deficit. Fetal monitoring. Clinical bleeding endpoint.
cautions: Warfarin in T1 / T3: teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy) / fetal intracranial bleed risk. In a mechanical valve patient on warfarin: confer with cardiology before stopping — switch to LMWH at therapeutic dose was the standard during pregnancy but recurrent thrombosis on LMWH led to some experts continuing warfarin T2 weeks 13-36.
DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
TXA is safe in pregnancy (WOMAN trial supports use within 3 h of PPH).

protocols.agent: Hold LMWH 12-24 h; protamine if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Prophylactic LMWH: hold 12 h pre-procedure. Therapeutic LMWH: hold 24 h. Protamine if intra-procedural bleeding.
Hold LMWH. Local haemostasis. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV.
Hold; obstetric review; reassess weight-based dosing (weight gain in pregnancy may shift dose).

pitfalls: Warfarin embryopathy T1 (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) — avoid in T1.
DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Protamine only partially reverses LMWH — anticipate ongoing anti-Xa activity.
Hypercoagulability of pregnancy + post-bleed inflammatory state → high VTE recurrence risk; restart anticoagulation as soon as feasible.
Neuraxial anaesthesia + LMWH: hold ≥ 24 h (therapeutic) / ≥ 12 h (prophylactic) before block.

references.label: WOMAN Trial Collaborators. Effect of early tranexamic acid administration on mortality, hysterectomy, and other morbidities in women with postpartum haemorrhage (WOMAN trial). Lancet 2017;389:2105-16.
RCOG Green-top Guideline 37a: Reducing the risk of venous thromboembolism during pregnancy and the puerperium.

drugClass: Antifibrinolytic — special-case scenario where TXA is the wrong tool
oneLiner: TXA reduces fibrinolysis — useful in trauma / PPH / surgical bleed but harmful when active thrombosis or DIC with secondary fibrinolysis. Subarachnoid haemorrhage: TXA may worsen ischaemia. Active VTE: contraindicated. Haematuria from upper urinary tract: ureteric clot obstruction risk.
mechanism: Tranexamic acid is a lysine analogue that binds plasminogen, blocking conversion to plasmin and preventing fibrin breakdown. Useful when bleeding is driven by hyperfibrinolysis; harmful when secondary fibrinolysis is a protective response to ongoing thrombosis (DIC, active VTE, MI, SAH).

protocols.agent: TXA appropriate ONLY in specific scenarios — withhold otherwise
protocols.dosing: Bleeding scenarios where TXA IS indicated: trauma within 3 h (CRASH-2), PPH within 3 h (WOMAN), mucosal / dental bleeding, ENT, ortho. Bleeding scenarios where TXA is CONTRAINDICATED or relatively contraindicated: active VTE / arterial thrombosis, DIC with consumptive coagulopathy, upper-tract haematuria (ureteric clot obstruction risk), subarachnoid haemorrhage > 24 h (controversial; older meta-analysis suggested ischaemic stroke risk), seizure disorder (TXA lowers seizure threshold at high doses, especially in cardiac surgery).
adjuncts: If TXA inadvertently given to a patient with active thrombosis: anticoagulation review, monitor for ischaemic events.
Seizures within hours of TXA + cardiac surgery: anticipate; manage with benzodiazepines.
protocols.monitoring: VTE surveillance, neurological observations.
cautions: Do not give TXA empirically without considering the bleeding mechanism.
Avoid in active arterial thrombosis (acute MI, ischaemic stroke without ICH).
Renal impairment dose-reduce (CrCl 30-60: 50% dose; 10-30: 25% dose).
Caution in elderly + cardiac surgery + high-dose TXA: seizure risk.

protocols.agent: TXA prophylaxis in selected surgery; avoid in pro-thrombotic patients
protocols.dosing: Orthopaedic / cardiac / spinal / cranial / obstetric surgery: TXA 1 g IV pre-incision then 1 g over 8 h (or per local protocol). Avoid in patients with active VTE or recent arterial event.
Mucosal / dental: TXA 4.8% mouthwash 10 mL, swill 2 min q6h, do not swallow. Menorrhagia: 1 g PO TDS during menses (5 days).

pitfalls: Empirical TXA in unclassified bleeding is not always safe — confirm bleeding mechanism is not thrombotic-protective fibrinolysis.
Upper-tract haematuria + TXA: clot retention, ureteric obstruction.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage + TXA: trial evidence mixed; modern practice individualises.
High-dose TXA in cardiac surgery + elderly: seizure risk.
Renal dose-adjustment essential — accumulation prolongs effect.

references.label: CRASH-2 trial collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, vascular occlusive events, and blood transfusion in trauma patients with significant haemorrhage. Lancet 2010;376:23-32.
WOMAN Trial Collaborators. Lancet 2017;389:2105-16.

oneLiner: HIT is a paradoxical thrombotic disorder requiring alternative anticoagulation. STOP all heparin (including LMWH and flushes). Start argatroban (hepatic clearance) or bivalirudin (renal); fondaparinux off-label in stable. Bleeding in HIT: stop drug + supportive; avoid platelet transfusion unless absolutely needed.
mechanism: HIT is an immune reaction to heparin-PF4 complexes producing IgG antibodies that activate platelets, causing both thrombocytopenia and paradoxical pro-thrombotic state. Alternative anticoagulant choice depends on organ function and bleeding risk.

protocols.agent: Stop alternative anticoagulant; supportive (avoid platelet transfusion if possible)
protocols.dosing: Stop argatroban / bivalirudin / fondaparinux immediately — short half-lives mean effect dissipates rapidly. Supportive: red cells, FFP, tranexamic acid. Recombinant factor VIIa 90 µg/kg IV as last resort. Platelet transfusion is RELATIVELY CONTRAINDICATED in HIT (theoretical risk of fuelling thrombosis) — give only if life-threatening bleeding and no alternative.
adjuncts: Local haemostasis.
Discuss with haematology — consider IVIG (high-dose, 1 g/kg/day × 2 days) for severe refractory HIT-related thrombosis with bleeding diathesis.
Reverse lethal triad.
protocols.monitoring: Platelet count daily until > 150 × 10⁹/L sustained. Anti-Xa or aPTT depending on agent. Doppler / imaging for new thrombosis (incidence 20-50% in confirmed HIT).
cautions: DO NOT restart any heparin product (including flushes, heparin-coated lines) — re-exposure can cause anaphylactoid reaction and severe thrombosis.
Platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated — risk of fuelling thrombosis; reserve for life-threatening bleed only.
Avoid warfarin alone in acute HIT — risk of venous limb gangrene; must overlap with non-heparin anticoagulant until platelet count normalised + INR therapeutic.
Argatroban interferes with INR — bridging to warfarin technically demanding.

protocols.dosing: Bivalirudin infusion adjusted by aPTT 1.5-2.5x baseline. Stop infusion 1-2 h pre-procedure. Argatroban alternative if hepatic clearance preferred.
Pause or halve argatroban / bivalirudin infusion. Local haemostasis.
Halve infusion rate; recheck aPTT in 1-2 h.

pitfalls: Failing to STOP all heparin (including flushes, heparin-bonded lines) — re-exposure worsens HIT.
Starting warfarin alone in acute HIT — risk of venous limb gangrene from protein C / S depletion; must bridge with non-heparin anticoagulant.
Platelet transfusion routinely in HIT is contraindicated — theoretical thrombosis fuel.
Argatroban dosing in hepatic impairment: start at 0.5 µg/kg/min (vs standard 2 µg/kg/min) — accumulation causes major bleeding.
Fondaparinux is off-label for acute HIT but commonly used in stable patients — limited evidence.

references.label: Cuker A et al. American Society of Hematology 2018 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv 2018;2:3360-92.
Linkins LA et al. Treatment and prevention of HIT (CHEST). 2012;141(2 Suppl):e495S-e530S.

oneLiner: Renal impairment (CrCl 15-49) extends rivaroxaban half-life — bleeding can persist 24+ h. 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg first-line where andexanet unavailable. Dialysis NOT effective (highly protein-bound). Activated charcoal up to 8 h post-ingestion.
mechanism: Rivaroxaban has ~ 33% renal clearance — CrCl 15-49 doubles AUC; CrCl < 15 not licensed. Half-life extends from 5-13 h (normal) to 9-13 h (CrCl 15-49) and longer in dialysis. Highly protein-bound (~ 95%) — not dialysable.

protocols.dosing: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg IV (max 5,000 IU). Andexanet alfa: standard dosing applies BUT renal impairment + drug-level persistence means high dose (800 mg bolus + 8 mg/min) often more appropriate; consult haematology. Activated charcoal 50 g PO/NG within 8 h.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid.
Stop rivaroxaban; reassess indication.
Reverse lethal triad.
protocols.monitoring: Rivaroxaban-calibrated anti-Xa (drawn pre-PCC and 30 min post for trend). Clinical bleeding. Note andexanet interferes with anti-Xa.
cautions: Dialysis is NOT effective for rivaroxaban removal (highly protein-bound) — do not use.
Andexanet effect ends within 1-2 h of stopping infusion; rebleeding from redistributed drug is possible especially in renal impairment.
Renal impairment + supratherapeutic dosing is a common cause of bleeding — confirm dose was appropriate.

protocols.agent: Hold longer than normal renal function; 4F-PCC if cannot delay
protocols.dosing: Standard bleed risk + CrCl 15-49: hold 48 h. High bleed risk + CrCl 15-49: hold 72 h. Urgent: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg or andexanet.
Hold rivaroxaban. Charcoal within 8 h. 4F-PCC if bleeding persists.
Hold 1-2 doses. Reassess dose (15 mg OD for CrCl 15-49 in AF; 20 mg OD for CrCl ≥ 50 with food).

pitfalls: Renal impairment + standard dose = supratherapeutic — confirm prescribing.
Dialysis ineffective (protein binding).
Andexanet effect short-lived — anticipate rebleeding from residual drug.
8-h activated charcoal window (longer than apixaban) — useful even in late presentations.

references.label: ANNEXA-4 (Connolly et al. NEJM 2019).
EHRA 2021 practical guide on NOAC use in AF, renal impairment section.

anticoagulant: Reversal antidote inventory — availability + dosing reference
oneLiner: Quick-reference inventory: idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet alfa (apixaban / rivaroxaban), 4F-PCC (warfarin + DOAC-Xa), vitamin K, protamine, cryoprecipitate, tranexamic acid, bentracimab (ticagrelor — where available).
mechanism: Each reversal agent works on a different target — knowing what is on the shelf (and what is not) is itself a patient-safety decision.

protocols.dosing: IDARUCIZUMAB (Praxbind) — dabigatran: 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials, 15 min apart). Onset minutes. Stocked: tertiary EDs, anticoagulation centres. ANDEXANET ALFA (Andexxa, Ondexxya) — apixaban / rivaroxaban: low dose 400 mg bolus + 4 mg/min × 120 min OR high dose 800 mg bolus + 8 mg/min × 120 min, depending on last dose + time. Stocked: select centres; expensive ($25-50k per course). 4F-PCC (Beriplex, Kcentra, Octaplex) — warfarin / DOAC-Xa: 25-50 IU/kg IV. Universally stocked. VITAMIN K (phytomenadione) — warfarin: 1-5 mg PO (non-bleed); 5-10 mg IV slow (bleed). Universal. PROTAMINE — UFH (full reversal), LMWH (partial): 1 mg/100 units UFH or 1 mg/mg enoxaparin (time-adjusted). Universal. CRYOPRECIPITATE — fibrinolytics / hypofibrinogenaemia: 10 units IV; aim fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L. TRANEXAMIC ACID — adjunctive in major bleed: 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h. Universal, cheap. BENTRACIMAB (PB2452) — ticagrelor: 18 g IV per labelling (loading bolus + 4 h infusion). Availability limited.
adjuncts: Stocking decisions: pharmacy should hold idarucizumab + 4F-PCC + vitamin K + protamine + cryoprecipitate + tranexamic acid as baseline; andexanet at tertiary anticoagulation centres.
Cold-chain: idarucizumab and andexanet refrigerated; 4F-PCC room-temp lyophilised.
Reconstitution time: 4F-PCC 5-10 min; idarucizumab ready-to-use vial; andexanet requires reconstitution (~ 30 min for full course).
Cost: andexanet > $25,000 per course (major barrier); 4F-PCC ~ $3,000-5,000; idarucizumab ~ $4,000-5,000.
protocols.monitoring: Local audit of antidote stock + expiry, time-to-drug metrics for major bleed pathways.
cautions: Many smaller centres lack idarucizumab / andexanet — confirm what is in YOUR pharmacy before assuming availability.
Reconstitution delay can negate the benefit — pre-mixed andexanet protocols (high-dose ready-to-use) reduce time-to-effect.
Expiry tracking — these are low-throughput high-cost agents that lapse.

protocols.agent: Confirm antidote availability pre-emptively for high-risk patients
protocols.dosing: When a patient on a DOAC presents for surgery, confirm specific reversal availability BEFORE inducing anaesthesia.

pitfalls: Assuming andexanet is on the shelf — many EDs do not stock it.
Confusing 4F-PCC with FFP — they are not interchangeable; 4F-PCC is the correct agent.
Expired stock — low-throughput agents often lapse; pharmacy must rotate.
Time-to-reconstitution is a hidden delay — practice runs in major haemorrhage simulations recommended.
Bentracimab availability is highly variable globally — confirm local stock.

references.label: Tomaselli GF et al. 2020 ACC expert consensus on management of bleeding in patients on oral anticoagulants. JACC 2020.
ISTH guidance: When and how to use idarucizumab and andexanet alfa. J Thromb Haemost 2020.

anticoagulant: Subcutaneous prophylactic UFH (5,000 units BD/TDS) — bleed
oneLiner: Prophylactic-dose subcutaneous UFH causes far less anticoagulation than IV therapeutic dose. Most bleeding is supportive; protamine rarely needed. Check for HIT if thrombocytopenia.
mechanism: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and lower bioavailability (~ 30%) than IV; aPTT often normal at prophylactic dose. Anti-Xa activity modest. HIT risk is similar at prophylactic vs therapeutic dose.

protocols.dosing: Stop UFH. Protamine ONLY if aPTT prolonged or anti-Xa elevated — typically 1 mg per 100 units of UFH given in last 8 h (lower for time since dose). Often supportive measures alone suffice. Check platelets for HIT.
adjuncts: Red cells, FFP, platelets per haemorrhage protocol.
Local haemostasis.
Check anti-PF4 / functional HIT testing if platelets dropped > 50% from baseline within 5-14 days of starting heparin.
protocols.monitoring: aPTT, anti-Xa (heparin-calibrated), platelet count. Clinical bleeding.
cautions: If HIT is suspected — STOP all heparin including LMWH and flushes; switch to argatroban / bivalirudin (see hit-anticoagulation-choice).
Protamine doses larger than the heparin dose are themselves anticoagulant — do not over-dose.

protocols.agent: Hold next dose; usually safe to proceed at 8-12 h
protocols.dosing: Hold next dose; effect usually dissipates within 8-12 h. Protamine rarely needed pre-procedure for prophylactic-dose UFH.
Stop UFH. Local haemostasis.
Hold next dose; reassess weight + renal function.

pitfalls: Failing to consider HIT in a bleeding patient with thrombocytopenia on UFH.
Over-dosing protamine — itself anticoagulant.
Subcutaneous UFH bioavailability is variable — aPTT can be unreliable; anti-Xa more accurate.

references.label: BSH guideline 2018.
Cuker A et al. ASH 2018 HIT guideline.

drugClass: Direct oral anticoagulants — intentional overdose scenario
oneLiner: Massive DOAC ingestion: activated charcoal early (apixaban 2-4 h, rivaroxaban 8 h, dabigatran 2 h); haemodialysis ONLY for dabigatran (others highly protein-bound). Specific reversal (idarucizumab / andexanet) if bleeding develops; supportive otherwise.
mechanism: Most DOAC overdoses do not cause immediate bleeding — drug effect is determined by absorption + clearance. Activated charcoal interrupts absorption; dialysis removes dabigatran (low protein binding) but not apixaban / rivaroxaban / edoxaban (highly protein-bound).

protocols.dosing: Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV + dialysis (removes ~ 60% in 4 h). Apixaban / rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa (high dose if recent ingestion: 800 mg + 8 mg/min) OR 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg. Edoxaban / betrixaban: 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg. Activated charcoal 50 g PO/NG if within absorption window.
adjuncts: Red cells, platelets, tranexamic acid.
Psychiatric review for intent; safety plan.
Toxicology consult.
protocols.monitoring: Anti-Xa (drug-specific calibration), aPTT, INR. Clinical bleeding. Re-bleeding monitor for 24-48 h (drug redistribution).
cautions: DOAC overdose without bleeding does NOT routinely require reversal — supportive observation with surveillance is reasonable.
Dialysis only useful for dabigatran (low protein binding); others not dialysable.
Activated charcoal contraindicated if airway not protected.

protocols.dosing: Idarucizumab / andexanet / 4F-PCC as per agent.
Charcoal within agent-specific window. Local haemostasis. 4F-PCC 25-50 IU/kg if persistent.
Charcoal if within window. Observation for ≥ 24 h (re-absorption / delayed bleed). Psychiatric review.

pitfalls: Empirical reversal for asymptomatic DOAC overdose is unnecessary and exposes to procoagulant risk.
Charcoal window: apixaban 2-4 h, rivaroxaban up to 8 h, dabigatran 2 h.
Dabigatran is dialysable; other DOACs are not.
Intentional overdose: do not forget psychiatric review + safety plan.
Concomitant ingestions (paracetamol, NSAIDs) common — screen broadly.

references.label: ACMT position statement: Use of specific reversal agents for direct oral anticoagulant overdose. J Med Toxicol 2020.
ISTH guidance 2020.

oneLiner: INR 4.5-10 without bleed: hold 1-2 doses, recheck — do NOT routinely give vitamin K. INR > 10 without bleed: vitamin K 1-5 mg PO. INR < 4.5 + no bleed: reduce or skip 1 dose. Inappropriate vitamin K causes prolonged sub-therapeutic INR.
mechanism: Supratherapeutic INR without bleeding has a low absolute bleed risk in the short term; warfarin reversal that is too aggressive produces a window of under-anticoagulation and thromboembolic risk.

protocols.agent: If bleeding develops: treat as warfarin major bleed
protocols.dosing: 4F-PCC + vitamin K — see warfarin-reversal.

INR < 4.5 + no bleed: omit / reduce next dose. INR 4.5-10 + no bleed: hold 1-2 doses; routine vitamin K NOT recommended (ACCP 2018). INR > 10 + no bleed: hold + vitamin K 1-5 mg PO; recheck INR at 24 h. Restart at lower dose when therapeutic. Identify precipitant (antibiotic, diet change, missed dose, adherence).
adjuncts: Identify precipitating factor — most supratherapeutic INRs have a cause (antibiotic interaction, illness, dietary change, dosing error).
Counsel patient on cause + future avoidance.
protocols.monitoring: INR daily until therapeutic.
cautions: Avoid IV / IM vitamin K — anaphylactoid reactions; PO is reliable and predictable.
Avoid SC vitamin K — erratic absorption.
Large vitamin K doses (≥ 10 mg) cause prolonged warfarin resistance — use 1-5 mg PO.

pitfalls: Routinely giving vitamin K for INR 4.5-10 without bleed is harmful (induces sub-therapeutic INR) — hold dose is enough.
SC vitamin K — erratic; do not use.
Failing to identify the precipitant (antibiotic, illness, dietary change) misses the root cause.
Large vitamin K doses cause days of warfarin resistance — use minimum dose.

references.label: ACCP CHEST 2018 antithrombotic therapy guideline.
BSH guideline 2018.

drugClass: Reversal adjunct for vitamin K antagonists
oneLiner: Choose route by urgency: IV (5-10 mg, diluted, over ≥ 30 min) with PCC for major bleed; oral (1-5 mg) for supratherapeutic INR without bleeding. Avoid SC (erratic) and never give undiluted IV bolus (anaphylactoid risk).
mechanism: Phytomenadione is the cofactor for hepatic γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S. It restores endogenous synthesis of functional factors over 4-6 h (IV) to 24 h (oral) — it does NOT replace factors directly, so it is an adjunct, not a stand-alone agent, for active major bleeding.

protocols.dosing: 5-10 mg IV, diluted, infused slowly (manufacturer max rate 1 mg/min; in practice infuse over ≥ 30 min) — always co-administered with 4F-PCC. Vitamin K sustains reversal once the PCC factors decay (PCC duration up to ~ 8 h); without it, INR rebounds at 12-24 h.
adjuncts: 4F-PCC dosed by INR/weight for the actual reversal — vitamin K alone is too slow for life-threatening bleeding.
Manage anaphylactoid reaction (rare, ~ 3 per 10,000 IV doses): stop infusion, adrenaline, IV fluids.
protocols.monitoring: INR begins to fall within 4-6 h of IV vitamin K; recheck at 6 h and 24 h.
cautions: Never give undiluted rapid IV bolus — anaphylactoid reactions are associated with rapid infusion.
Subcutaneous vitamin K is unreliable (erratic absorption) — do not use for reversal.

protocols.dosing: Oral phytomenadione 1-2.5 mg lowers an INR of 5-9 into range within 24-48 h; for INR > 10 without bleeding, 5 mg PO may be more appropriate. Oral route is preferred when no major bleed because IV carries anaphylactoid risk and SC is erratic.
cautions: Avoid large doses (≥ 10 mg) in patients needing ongoing warfarin — causes prolonged warfarin resistance for days.

pitfalls: Vitamin K alone takes 4-6 h (IV) or up to 24 h (oral) to act — never rely on it for active life-threatening bleeding; give PCC for the acute reversal.
Subcutaneous administration is erratic and should not be used.
Failing to co-administer vitamin K with PCC leads to INR rebound at 12-24 h as PCC factors decay.
Routine vitamin K for INR 4.5-10 without bleeding is unnecessary and can cause sub-therapeutic INR — holding the dose usually suffices.

references.label: Ageno W et al. ACCP CHEST: Oral anticoagulant therapy. Chest 2012;141(2 Suppl):e44S-e88S.
BSH guideline: Reversal of antithrombotic therapy in patients with major bleeding. Br J Haematol 2018.

oneLiner: Single dose desmopressin 0.3 micrograms/kg IV over ~ 30 min for uraemic bleeding or antiplatelet-associated haemorrhage (including ICH). Effect lasts 4-6 h; restrict fluids and watch for hyponatraemia.
mechanism: Desmopressin releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial stores, improving platelet adhesion. It improves platelet function in uraemia and partially counteracts the platelet defect from antiplatelet agents (e.g. aspirin).

protocols.dosing: 0.3 micrograms/kg IV in 50 mL normal saline over ~ 30 min, single dose. Current neurocritical care guidance gives a conditional recommendation to consider a single dose of IV desmopressin for antiplatelet-associated intracranial haemorrhage (low-quality evidence). Same dose improves platelet function in uraemic bleeding.
adjuncts: For antiplatelet-associated ICH: do NOT routinely add platelet transfusion (PATCH signal of harm).
Treat the underlying uraemia (dialysis, correct anaemia) for sustained benefit.
Local haemostasis, blood-pressure control, neurosurgical consult for ICH.
protocols.monitoring: Effect lasts ~ 4-6 h. Monitor serum sodium — repeated dosing causes hyponatraemia / water intoxication.
cautions: Mandatory fluid restriction to prevent hyponatraemia, especially in elderly / uraemic patients.
Tachyphylaxis: repeated doses lose effect as endothelial stores deplete.
Use cautiously in unstable cardiovascular disease (vasodilation, hypotension on rapid infusion).

pitfalls: Desmopressin is an adjunct, not a primary reversal agent — it does not replace specific anticoagulant reversal.
Hyponatraemia from antidiuretic effect can precipitate seizures — restrict free water and monitor sodium.
Evidence for antiplatelet-associated ICH is low quality (conditional recommendation) — weigh against thrombotic risk.
Tachyphylaxis after ~ 1-2 doses limits repeat use.

references.label: Frontera JA et al. Neurocritical Care Society / SCCM Guideline for reversal of antithrombotics in intracranial haemorrhage. Neurocrit Care 2016;24:6-46.
Kapapa M et al. Effect of desmopressin on platelet dysfunction during antiplatelet therapy: a systematic review. Neurocrit Care 2020.

oneLiner: Do NOT routinely transfuse platelets for spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage in patients on antiplatelet therapy — the PATCH trial showed harm (increased death/dependence). Reserve platelets for those proceeding to neurosurgery.
mechanism: Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors) impair platelet aggregation. Transfusing functional platelets was hypothesised to restore haemostasis, but the PATCH randomised trial found a signal of harm in spontaneous ICH.

protocols.agent: Avoid routine platelet transfusion (PATCH); consider only for neurosurgery
